title: QwenPU: An LLM running inside another LLM's weights
content:
Instructions to use divagr1925/QwenPU with libraries, inference providers, notebooks, and local apps. Follow these links to get started.
- Libraries
-  Transformers How to use divagr1925/QwenPU with Transformers: # Use a pipeline as a high-level helper
from transformers import pipeline
pipe = pipeline("text-generation", model="divagr1925/QwenPU")
messages = [
    {"role": "user", "content": "Who are you?"},
]
pipe(messages) # pip install -U transformers accelerate
# Load model directly
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForCausalLM
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("divagr1925/QwenPU")
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained("divagr1925/QwenPU", device_map="auto")
messages = [
    {"role": "user", "content": "Who are you?"},
]
inputs = tokenizer.apply_chat_template(
	messages,
	add_generation_prompt=True,
	tokenize=True,
	return_dict=True,
	return_tensors="pt",
).to(model.device)
outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=256)
print(tokenizer.decode(outputs[0][inputs["input_ids"].shape[-1]:]))

Code on GitHub · Qwenputer · Base model: Qwen/Qwen3.5-4B · Apache-2.0
QwenPU is Qwen3.5-4B with a 32-bit RISC-V CPU and a vector unit compiled into its weights. The vector unit runs a whole neural network inside the model's forward passes: Andrej Karpathy's stories260K, the 260K-parameter Llama from llama2.c, runs as a program on it and writes its stories.
It's part of Qwenputer: the same CPU, compiled into transformer layers in front of Qwen's own, every weight set by a compiler, with Qwen3.5's Gated DeltaNet state as its memory. Qwenputer-npu gave that CPU dot-product instructions. QwenPU gives it a vector unit of its own: separate memories in DeltaNet heads, 64-lane matrix rows a token, and whole vector results streamed through the token stream.
Work in progress. QwenPU is exact, but not yet small: the checkpoint is 26.7 GB, so it needs a 40 GB or larger GPU to load whole. The story demo and the checks run the computer's layers on their own and fit a 24 GB GPU. Trimming the hidden size, and with it the checkpoint, is next.
A language model inside the language model
stories260K is a C program here (guests/stories260k/stories_vx.c). Its int4 weights sit in the
vector unit's weight memory, loaded from the program, and every matrix row, residual add,
softmax and attention read is a vector op. None of it is compiled into the checkpoint, so any
model that fits runs the same way.
Every build writes the same story, token for token:
Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to play outside in the park. One day, she saw a big, red ball. She wanted to play with it, but it was too high
The vector unit
Its memories are DeltaNet heads: 16 vector registers of 64 words, 384 int8 activations, 4,152 row-chunks of int4 weights, and K / V caches for 32 positions. An op's record starts with config tokens carrying its operands, then streams its results, and each token is one exact step of the compiled layers. SiLU and exp are fixed-point function units, generic like the CPU's adders.
Checks
- Every vector op runs random test programs on this checkpoint's own chip layers, teacher-forced against a reference model of the unit, along with the first 30,000 steps of the story program: zero mismatches.
- The circuit's executor writes the whole story free-running on a GPU, checked against the reference at every one of its 3,184,920 steps: exact. It runs at about 3,300 trace tokens a second on an L4, so a story token takes about 16 seconds, against 41 for Qwenputer-npu.
Quickstart
git clone https://github.com/divagr18/QwenPU && cd QwenPU && uv sync --extra hf
uv run python guests/stories260k/storyrun.py guests/stories260k/stories_vx.elf --vx
hf download divagr1925/QwenPU --local-dir qwenpu
uv run python -m chipformer.rv.vxcheck qwenpu guests/stories260k/stories_vx.elf
storyrun writes the story on the computer's executor; vxcheck runs the vector unit on this
checkpoint's layers (--chip-only loads only those on the GPU, about 13 GB).

Apache-2.0. This is a modified version of Qwen/Qwen3.5-4B: the config is widened and computer layers are added, but Qwen's own weights are unchanged. stories260K and llama2.c are by Andrej Karpathy (MIT).

report.summary: QwenPU embeds a working 32-bit RISC-V CPU and vector unit into Qwen3.5-4B's weights, letting a tiny language model run as a program inside the host model's forward passes.
report.background: For years researchers have toyed with the idea that transformer weights might be a substrate for computation beyond pattern matching. Divyansh Agrawal's Qwenputer project pushes that idea literally: rather than prompting a model to simulate a computer, it compiles an actual CPU into extra transformer layers bolted in front of Qwen's own, with every weight set by a compiler. An earlier release, Qwenputer-npu, gave that CPU dot-product instructions. QwenPU adds a dedicated vector unit so the embedded machine can run real neural-network inference. The guest program is Andrej Karpathy's stories260K, the 260K-parameter Llama from llama2.c, whose int4 weights sit in the vector unit's memory rather than the checkpoint. The work lands in a broader wave of interest in mechanistic interpretability and 'computational' views of weights, but it is explicitly a work-in-progress research artifact, not a product.
key_points: A real CPU lives in the weights: QwenPU widens Qwen3.5-4B's config and adds layers implementing a 32-bit RISC-V core plus a vector unit, all weights produced by a compiler. Qwen's original weights are untouched; the checkpoint is Apache-2.0 and 26.7 GB.

A tiny LLM runs inside the big one: Karpathy's stories260K (260K parameters, int4) executes as a C program on the vector unit, performing every matrix row, residual add, softmax and attention read as vector ops. It writes a fixed children's story token for token, deterministically.

Memory is the model's own state: the vector unit borrows the Gated DeltaNet heads for storage, with 16 vector registers of 64 words, 384 int8 activations, 4,152 row-chunks of int4 weights, and K/V caches for 32 positions. Results stream out through the token stream.

Correctness is verified, speed is not: every vector op passed random tests with zero mismatches, and the full story ran free-running for all 3,184,920 steps exactly. On an L4 it manages roughly 3,300 trace tokens per second, meaning about 16 seconds per story token versus 41 for the earlier Qwenputer-npu.

It is heavy and unfinished: a 40 GB or larger GPU is needed to load the full checkpoint, though the demo and checks can run the computer's layers alone in about 13 GB on a 24 GB card. Shrinking the hidden size is the stated next step.
report.impact: This is less a practical tool than a proof of concept with genuine conceptual weight: it demonstrates that transformer weights can host a Turing-complete-ish machine and even a second neural network, executed exactly rather than approximated. For researchers, it opens a concrete experimental path for studying computation inside models and for hybrid architectures where symbolic programs and learned layers share a substrate. For developers, the near-term lesson is negative on cost: 26.7 GB checkpoints and 16 seconds per token are nowhere near production. But the pattern, compiling deterministic programs into unused capacity of a model, hints at future approaches for verifiable, sandboxed behaviour. For regular users, nothing changes yet, though 'a model that runs programs' is a useful corrective to the idea that LLMs only predict tokens.
report.tools: Follow the QwenPU GitHub repo (github.com/divagr18/QwenPU) and the Hugging Face model card (divagr1925/QwenPU); quickstart uses uv, Transformers, vLLM or SGLang. Read Andrej Karpathy's llama2.c and stories260K for the guest side, and explore Qwen3.5-4B as the host. Anyone interested in the underlying idea should also look at mechanistic interpretability tooling like TransformerLens, and at the earlier Qwenputer-npu release for comparison.
